text:
The question of who bears responsibility for the humanitarian consequences of U.S. immigration enforcement — including the detention of children and legal residents — is contested, with blame distributed across multiple actors and levels of government.

## The Trump Administration and Federal Agencies

The most direct responsibility lies with the Trump administration and its immigration enforcement agencies. ProPublica and congressional investigators documented over 170 U.S. citizens detained by immigration agents, including more than 20 children, with some citizen children actually deported [6]. Cases include a 7-year-old autistic Canadian-American girl detained at a Texas ICE facility under conditions her father described as involving sleeping on the floor with "tin space blanket things" and "terrible" food [10]. A 16-year-old U.S. citizen was "tackled and choked" by agents pursuing his undocumented father, placed in a chokehold and handcuffed [6].

The Department of Homeland Security has largely deflected responsibility. In response to the detention of the autistic girl, a DHS spokesperson stated bluntly: "Being in detention is a choice" [10]. DHS also denied specific allegations of abuse, claiming "ICE does not zip tie or handcuff children," even when detained families reported otherwise [6].

## Congressional and Political Responsibility

Democrats and Republicans in Congress share responsibility through legislative inaction and political maneuvering. Democrats have refused to fund DHS without restraints on immigration enforcement, while Republicans have resisted meaningful oversight [3][29]. Former ICE Director John Sandweg noted that deploying ICE agents to airports — itself a product of the DHS funding shutdown — was "unprecedented in the history of the agency" [24]. Senate Democrats have demanded reforms including body cameras, judicial warrants for home searches, and identification requirements for agents [29].

## State and Local Governments

Sanctuary city policies have also drawn criticism. In the case of an undocumented Venezuelan man accused of killing college student Sheridan Gorman, Chicago's sanctuary policies meant he was released after a shoplifting arrest without being turned over to ICE — a failure the victim's family called a "systemic failure within the immigration system" [15][5].

## Broader Accountability Gaps

A Senate minority staff report compiled 128 cases of children — citizens and noncitizens — "injured, left unattended or otherwise put at risk" by DHS enforcement operations [6]. Religious leaders, union officials, and civil society groups have widely condemned these practices. Imam Ayman Soliman, a legal resident detained for 73 days, stated: "They told us they were detaining and deporting the criminals... I have zero criminal record" [2]. Hospitality union Unite Here Local 11 cited "the detention of legal permanent residents and citizens" as evidence of "abhorrent" conditions justifying workers' right to refuse assignments near ICE agents [14].

In summary, responsibility is shared — primarily by the Trump administration and ICE for carrying out enforcement operations that have ensnared children and legal residents [6][10], by Congress for failing to pass oversight legislation [3][29], and in some cases by local sanctuary policies that critics argue enable dangerous individuals to remain in communities [15].
